turns.doctor_question: Have you ever had a period of several days or longer when you felt unusually euphoric or irritable?
turns.patient_response:
Euphoric? Or irritable? No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I get frustrated with the audits, obviously, but not like... unusually angry for days on end or anything. And definitely not euphoric. I'm just a regular guy trying to do my job. 

Though speaking of being irritable, you should have seen my old neighbor, Mr. Henderson, back when I lived in the suburbs. The man was perpetually angry about his lawn. He had this pristine Kentucky Bluegrass, and he'd be out there with actual scissors clipping the edges along the sidewalk. I swear, if a single dandelion popped up, he looked like he was going to have a stroke. He used to yell at the neighborhood kids just for riding their bikes too close to the curb. 

One time, the mail carrier accidentally stepped on the corner of his grass, and Henderson filed a formal complaint with the postmaster. Can you imagine having that kind of time on your hands? The post office is a whole other thing, though. Have you noticed how much a stamp costs these days? It's ridiculous. I remember when you could mail a letter for, what, 32 cents? Now they have those "Forever" stamps, which I guess is a smart marketing gimmick. My aunt Margaret used to collect stamps. She had these huge albums filled with them, all categorized by country and year. She had one from the 1939 World's Fair that she swore was worth a fortune, but when she passed away and my cousin tried to sell it, the dealer offered him like five bucks. 

Collectibles are a scam, if you ask me. People think Beanie Babies or comic books are going to fund their retirement, and then they end up with a basement full of junk. I try to keep things minimal, you know? Less clutter. But yeah, no, I haven't had any days where I felt super euphoric or overly irritable. Just normal, really.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's response demonstrates tangentiality and loose associations, drifting from his neighbor's lawn to the post office, stamps, and collectibles before returning to the original question.

Withdrawn? Losing interest? Well, I guess I haven't been going out much, but that's just because I need to keep an eye on things at home. You know, making sure my network is secure, checking the logs. I used to go to this bowling league on Thursday nights. The "Pin Pals," we called ourselves. Terrible name, I know, but Dave came up with it and he was the team captain, so we just went with it. 

Dave was a character. He drove this old AMC Gremlin, bright orange. You don't see those anymore. Actually, AMC had some really weird designs back in the day. The Pacer? Looked like a fishbowl on wheels. My dad had a Ford Pinto, which was another disaster waiting to happen. You know they designed those gas tanks so poorly that a rear-end collision could just... boom. turns.doctor_question: Have you had any major head injury, stroke, seizure, or other brain illness before these beliefs started?
turns.patient_response:
Head injury? Stroke? No, nothing like that. My brain works just fine, better than most, honestly, considering I'm the only one catching the discrepancies in the system. But no, I haven't had any seizures or strokes. 

My uncle Bob had a stroke, though. It was really sudden. He was just sitting in his recliner watching the Golf Channel—he loved golf, used to play 18 holes every Sunday at this public course down in Florida. Florida is so humid, I don't know how anyone lives there year-round. The humidity just ruins electronics. I went down to visit him once in August, and my laptop screen started getting condensation on the inside just from carrying it from the air-conditioned car to the house. 

Air conditioning is a marvel, really, when you think about it. Willis Carrier invented it, right? Originally it wasn't even for comfort, it was for a printing plant in Brooklyn to keep the paper from wrinkling in the humidity. Printing presses are fascinating machines. My high school had a shop class where we actually learned typesetting. You had to place every single letter backward on this tray. It took forever. We printed the school newspaper that way. Now, you just hit a button and a laser printer spits out thirty pages a minute. 

I bought a laser printer for my home office a few years back, a Brother model. Solid machine, never jams. Unlike those cheap inkjet ones where the ink costs more than the printer itself. It's a total racket. They sell you the printer at a loss and then gouge you on the cartridges. It's the razor-and-blades business model. Gillette perfected that a hundred years ago. I still use a safety razor, actually. Much cheaper, and a closer shave. You have to be careful not to nick yourself, though. 

But yeah, no head injuries or anything like that. My head is perfectly fine. I just need people to start looking at the data I've been pulling.

turns.patient_response:
Less sleep? No, I don't think so. I mean, I don't sleep great, but I definitely need it. I usually get about six, maybe seven hours if I'm lucky. Sometimes I'll wake up around 3 AM and just stare at the ceiling, thinking about work. 

You know, 3 AM is supposedly the "witching hour." I read this article once that said most people wake up at that time because it's when your body temperature drops to its lowest point. Or maybe it was a drop in blood sugar? I can't remember. I used to eat a bowl of cereal right before bed to try and keep my blood sugar stable. Cheerios, mostly. The plain ones, not the Honey Nut. Honey Nut has way too much sugar. 

Sugar is in everything now. Have you noticed that? Even bread. You buy a loaf of wheat bread and it's got high fructose corn syrup in it. It's terrible for you. My dentist was telling me last week that he's seeing more cavities in adults now than ever before. He's a nice guy, Dr. Patel. He has this massive fish tank in his waiting room. Saltwater, too, which I hear is incredibly difficult to maintain. You have to get the salinity just right, and if the temperature fluctuates even a little bit, all the fish die. 

I had a goldfish when I was a kid. Won it at a carnival by tossing a ping pong ball into a little glass bowl. I named him Jaws. He lived for surprisingly long, like four years. We just kept him in this little bowl on the kitchen counter. My mom would change the water every few days. She used to put a little bit of that blue liquid in there... water conditioner, I think it was called? To get rid of the chlorine from the tap water. 

Tap water is another thing. People buy bottled water, but half the time it's just filtered municipal water anyway. You're basically paying two dollars for a plastic bottle. The plastic waste is getting out of hand. I try to recycle, but I saw a documentary that said most of the stuff you put in the recycling bin just ends up in a landfill anyway. It's pretty depressing when you think about it. 

But yeah, sleep. No, I haven't had any days where I just didn't need to sleep. I'm usually pretty tired by the end of the day.

Vegas is such a strange city. It's just a massive monument to excess sitting right in the middle of a desert. The air conditioning in those casinos is freezing, though. You never know what time it is because there are no windows or clocks anywhere on the casino floor.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease, dementia, or another neurological or medical condition that affects the brain?

Parkinson's? Dementia? No, no, my brain is perfectly fine. I get a physical every year, bloodwork, the whole nine yards, and everything is completely normal. 

Although, speaking of medical stuff, the healthcare system in this country is just a nightmare to navigate. The billing alone is a full-time job. I had a minor procedure a few years back—just a little outpatient thing—and I got bills from the hospital, the doctor, the anesthesiologist, and some random lab I'd never even heard of. It's all because they use these different billing codes, and if one number is off, the insurance company just denies the whole claim. They use these automated algorithms now to flag claims for denial. It's not even a person looking at it most of the time. 

Algorithms are running everything now, honestly. They decide what you see on social media, what ads you get, even what price you pay for an airline ticket. Have you ever noticed that if you search for a flight a few times, the price suddenly goes up? They track your cookies and know you're interested, so they create artificial scarcity. It's a classic bait-and-switch. You really have to use a VPN and browse in incognito mode if you want to get a fair price on anything online these days. I set up a whole network-level ad blocker at my house using a Raspberry Pi. It's incredible how much junk it filters out. The internet is practically unusable without it now, just a constant barrage of pop-ups and tracking scripts. 

But no, to answer your question, I don't have any neurological conditions. My brain works just fine. I just need someone to take me seriously about these network logs.

Except now, with this whole situation at work, I'm staying late every night just trying to trace these unauthorized access attempts. It's exhausting. But no, nobody is reading my mind. I'm just trying to get people to look at the evidence I've found.
